title: AI careers deep dive
content_html:
What You'll Do

In this project you'll step into the shoes of three key AI professionals — the Machine Learning (ML) Engineer, the AI Ethicist, and the Data Scientist — to find out what they really do day to day, what skills and tools they use, and how their jobs connect (and sometimes clash) when a real AI system is built.

Instead of reading a dull job description, you'll use a chatbot as a "virtual career interviewee," asking it to role-play each professional. You'll run three mini-interviews, take notes, and then map out how these three roles would work together on one real project — for example, an app that recommends school subjects based on your grades. You'll finish by drawing a simple "career pipeline" showing who does what, and where tensions appear (like speed vs. fairness).

By the end you'll be able to name at least three AI careers, describe what each one is responsible for, and explain why ethics and data quality matter just as much as coding skill when building AI you can trust.

What You'll Need

  • A chatbot — ChatGPT (chat.openai.com) for the role-play interviews.
  • Somewhere to draw your pipeline — Google Slides (slides.google.com) or just paper and a pen.
  • Good to know: the free chatbot may be slow at busy times. If an answer is too technical, that's fine — you'll learn to ask it to simplify.

Steps

  1. Get the three roles straight: the ML Engineer builds and trains the models; the Data Scientist finds, cleans and analyses the data that feeds them; the AI Ethicist checks the system is fair, safe and respects people's rights.
  2. Pick a shared project to explore, e.g. "an app that recommends which school subjects a student should focus on, based on past grades and attendance."
  3. Interview each role in turn. Open ChatGPT and enter this, swapping in the role: "You are an experienced [ML Engineer / Data Scientist / AI Ethicist] working on a school subject recommendation app for teenagers in Nairobi. Explain in simple terms: (1) your main job on this project, (2) the tools or skills you use daily, (3) one challenge you might face, and (4) one question you'd ask the other team members before launching."
  4. If an answer is too jargon-heavy, add a follow-up: "Can you explain that like I'm 13?" Write each role's four answers in your own words.
  5. Draw a career pipeline: three boxes (e.g. Data Scientist → ML Engineer → AI Ethicist) with arrows showing what each hands to the next, and a note on each box saying "what could go wrong here."
  6. Present your pipeline in under 2 minutes, highlighting one interesting tension you found (e.g. the ML Engineer wants to launch fast, the Ethicist wants more testing).

Examples to Try

  • Notes sheet: "ML Engineer: I train the model on student data to predict good subject matches. I use Python and tools like scikit-learn. Challenge: not enough data from rural schools. Question for the team: do we have data from students like the ones who'll use this app?"
  • Pipeline diagram: [Data Scientist collects & cleans grade records] → [ML Engineer builds the model] → [AI Ethicist checks it's fair across genders/schools] → back to [Data Scientist to fix gaps]. Notes: "missing data," "model favours certain subjects," "who checks fairness before launch?"
  • Presentation line: "Our Ethicist refused to launch until the model was tested on at least three different types of school, because most of the training data came from just one."

Tips

  • Try at least two roles if you can — don't just take the easiest-sounding one.
  • Answers too similar across roles? Ask yourself why real professionals would differ more than the AI did — that's a clue about how the chatbot works.
  • Don't linger on the interviews. The diagram and the thinking about tensions are where the real learning is.
  • An analogy that helps: the Data Scientist is like a chef sourcing and prepping ingredients, the ML Engineer is the chef cooking, and the Ethicist is the food-safety inspector.

Think About It

  • What's the main difference between what a Data Scientist does and what an ML Engineer does?
  • Why might an AI Ethicist slow down a project others want to launch fast?
  • Could one person do all three jobs on a small team? What might be lost if they did?
  • Where in your pipeline was the most disagreement between roles? Why there?
  • If you could hire only one of the three for a small project on a tight budget, who would it be and why?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Interview a fourth role the same way (e.g. "AI Product Manager" or "Data Annotator") and add it to your pipeline.
  • Medium: Find a real job posting for one of these roles and compare it to what the chatbot said — what did the AI get right, and what did it leave out?
  • Hard: Write a 150–200 word "day in the life" from one role's view, about a week when a fairness problem is found just before launch — show how the three roles talk it through, including one disagreement and how it's settled.
